Functional Movement Science (HAS4867)
Measurement of Range of Motion (ROM)
Range of Motion can be defined as the amount of motion available at a joint.
Each specific joint has a normal range of motion that is expressed in degrees.
Universal goniometer is commonly used for measuring ROM.
Universal Goniometer
A universal goniometer is made of metal or plastic and it has three parts:
1. Body
2. Stationary arm
3. Moving arm
The body of the goniometer is like a protractor and may form a full or half circle,
with the scale from 0 - 180° or 360°. The axis is at the center of the body that
allows the moving arm to move freely on the body of the device.
The axis and body is placed over the joint being measured.
The stationary arm will be aligned with the inactive part of the joint measured
while the moving arm is placed on the part of the limb, which is moved in the
joint’s motion.

Subject test position

• Subject Supine
• Shoulder 90° abduction
• Forearm neutral
• Elbow fixed 90°
• Stabilize arm Goniometer Alignment
• Axis – olecranon process of ulna
• Stationary arm – aligned vertically
• Moving arm – aligned with ulna (styloid process) Action Ask the subject to rotate the arm down to the direction of the feet 5. Shoulder External Rotation Subject Test Position
• Subject Supine
• Shoulder 90° abduction
• Forearm neutral
• Elbow fixed 90°
• Stabilize arm Goniometer Alignment
• Axis – olecranon process of ulna
• Stationary arm – aligned vertically
• Moving arm – aligned with ulna (styloid process) Action Ask the subject to rotate the arm down to the direction of the head

text:
Ask the subject to flex the hip
2. Hip Extension
Subject Test Position
• Subject Prone
• Stabilize Pelvis Goniometer Alignment
• Axis – greater trochanter
• Stationary arm – aligned with midline of pelvis
• Moving arm – aligned with femur (lateral epicondyle) Action Ask the subject to extend the hip 3. Hip Abduction Subject Test Position
• Subject supine
• Stabilize pelvis to prevent pelvic list Goniometer Alignment
• Axis – anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS)
• Stationary arm – aligned with opposite ASIS
• Moving arm – aligned with femur (center of patella) Action Ask the subject to abduct the hip 4. Hip Internal Rotation Subject Test Position
• Subject sitting on high plinth
• Knee flexed
• Stabilize thigh Goniometer Alignment
• Axis – center of patella
• Stationary arm – aligned vertically
• Moving arm – aligned with leg (crest of tibia) Action Ask the subject to internal rotate the hip 5. Hip External Rotation Subject Test Position
• Subject sitting on high plinth
• Knee flexed
• Stabilize thigh Goniometer Alignment
• Axis – center of patella

text:
2. Plantarflexion
Subject Test Position
• Subject sitting in high plinth Goniometer Alignment
• Axis – lateral malleolus
• Stationary arm – aligned with fibular head
• Moving arm – aligned with fifth metatarsal Action Ask the subject to plantarflex the ankle 3. Inversion Subject Test Position
• Subject supine
• Stabilize calcaneus and talus Goniometer Alignment
• Axis – automatically positioned by alignment of goniometer arms
• Stationary arm – aligned with midline of leg
• Moving arm – aligned with plantar aspect of metatarsal heads Action Ask the subject to invert the forefoot 4. Eversion Subject Test Position
• Subject supine
• Stabilize calcaneus and talus Goniometer Alignment
• Axis – automatically positioned by alignment of goniometer arms
• Stationary arm – aligned with midline of leg
• Moving arm – aligned with plantar aspect of metatarsal heads Action Ask the subject to evert the forefoot
